Research project · 2026 · work in progress

Low-temperature plasma CFD in two codes

I implemented the plasma-fluid model of a doctoral thesis on an atmospheric-pressure helium plasma jet (Lazarou, University of Cyprus, 2019) in Ansys CFX 2025 R2 and in OpenFOAM v1912, so that each code checks the other. CFX has no plasma model, so the charged-particle transport and the field coupling are developed and verified here as CEL and User Fortran routines. The barrier-discharge model has run for six voltage periods in both codes; the two-dimensional jet is running on a refined mesh.

Overview

A plasma jet model that CFX cannot run as shipped

The reference is the helium plasma jet of Lazarou (University of Cyprus, 2019): a dielectric tube, a powered electrode and a dielectric slab, with a helium flow mixing into air. The model couples drift and diffusion of electrons, ions and excited species to Poisson's equation and an electron energy equation. Electron coefficients come from the Boltzmann solver BOLSIG+, and surface charge accumulates on the dielectric layers. The barrier discharge carries 12 species and 46 reactions; the jet carries 16 species and 93 reactions.

CFX 2025 R2 has no plasma model. Its algebraic-slip drift uses a first-order upwind flux and ignores the diffusivity, so a drift source undershoots at cell Péclet numbers above 2. It has no semi-implicit field coupling, and it defers part of the drift term to the previous coefficient loop. The dielectric relaxation time of about 0.25 ns then holds the time step for about 100 µs after every breakdown. The six periods of the barrier discharge would take about 49 days of CPU time (an estimate; the run was never made).

The project therefore builds the missing physics in CFX and builds an independent OpenFOAM model of the same equations, so that the two codes can be compared case by case.

Approach

One model, two routes

Both codes start from the same benchmarks: helium–air jet mixing, and an electron avalanche checked against its analytic solution. The barrier discharge comes before the jet.

Route 1 · Ansys CFX 2025 R2

CEL and User Fortran

Charged-particle drift is built from CFX's algebraic-slip model with a Scharfetter–Gummel diffusivity, which is exact on a cell Péclet number of 100 test layer. User Fortran routines couple the electric field semi-implicitly and solve the drift implicitly, so the dielectric-relaxation limit of about 0.25 ns no longer sets the step. Steps of up to 100 ns between discharges give six periods in 6.7 days of CPU time.

The routines target uniform structured meshes. Electron coefficients enter as tables from BOLSIG+. The jet User Fortran runs partitioned: equal to the serial run within solver tolerance, 1.5 times faster on two cores and 1.9 times on four.

Route 2 · OpenFOAM v1912

Seven C++ extensions of ltpFoam

The ltpFoam low-temperature plasma solver is extended with a pulsed voltage drive, the thesis's wall fluxes, a time-step limit, two-dimensional electron tables, meshed dielectrics and electrodes, closed boundaries and gas advection. About 3 900 lines of patches build the solver variants in order.

Each extension is tested to reproduce the previous solver byte for byte when switched off. All OpenFOAM runs use ESI v1912 in a Linux container; the comparisons with CFX are post-processed separately.

Shared inputs

Same physics, same tables

Both codes take the same reaction tables, electron transport and rate coefficients from BOLSIG+ 07/2024, and the same mesh nodes for the jet. The jet's reaction sources agree between OpenFOAM and CFX to 3 × 10-13 over 91 states and 16 species.

The jet mesh is refined to 20 µm cells along its path, because the ionisation front proved thinner than the original cells.

Verification

Each building block is checked before the whole

  • Analytic solution. The helium-gap avalanche matches its analytic solution within 0.04 % up to 2 ns; the electron cloud widths are 57.45 and 57.58 µm against 57.45 µm.
  • Manufactured solutions. The Scharfetter–Gummel drift is exact on a Péclet-number-100 layer (errors of 1.6 × 10-14 and 2 × 10-12) and second order in a field shaped by fixed space charge. In two dimensions the direction-dependent closure is second order along the mesh and at 30° to it (order 1.93; 1.81 on a graded mesh).
  • Gauss's law and charge conservation. Surface-charge tests give pure Laplace potentials exactly; net charge stays below 0.63 % of the ion charge. In the barrier discharge, net charge stays within 2 × 10-6 of the surface charge.
  • Implicit drift solver. The solver reproduces CFX's own node equations to 6 × 10-9. On the first pulse it gives 17.83 mA against 17.87 mA with the same onset.
  • Time-step studies. The OpenFOAM first pulse converges at a 0.02 ns cap; refinements of the step agree within 0.02 %. In CFX the breakdown onset moved by 0.60 µs between ionisation-step constants of 0.05 and 0.025.
  • Restarts and switches. CFX restarts equal the uninterrupted run bit for bit through the first step, and each OpenFOAM extension reproduces the previous solver byte for byte when switched off, on 623 to 734 output files per comparison.
  • CFX against OpenFOAM, barrier discharge. With the thesis's form of the electron energy, the first period agrees within 1.8 % in peak current and 0.7 % in charge. Over periods 2 to 4 the peaks agree within 7.2 % (charges within 6.3 %), with discharge onsets up to 1.8 µs apart.
  • CFX against OpenFOAM, jet. Over the first 22 ns, both codes at the same 0.1 ns step cap, the electron density where the discharge forms agrees within 0.1 %.
Limits stated once. The six periods have not yet become periodic in timing. In period 5, CFX splits the rising pulse into two discharges where OpenFOAM has one. The CFX main run adds an assumed stabiliser to the mean energy that raises the first pulse from about 10.7 to 18.0 mA, so only the runs without it are compared with OpenFOAM. Agreement with the thesis's own sixth-period currents is not claimed: OpenFOAM's peaks are about 20 % below the thesis's simulated values and the CFX main run's are 33 % and 69 % above them.

Results

Benchmarks, verification and the cross-code comparison

Status and next steps

The jet is running

  • September 2026
    Study of low-temperature plasma physics begins.
  • November 2026, first week
    Modelling starts in CFX with the two benchmarks, helium jet mixing and the electron avalanche, and the first technical reports.
  • 9 to 12 November 2026
    Semi-implicit field coupling and the implicit drift solver developed; first full discharge period run with charge conserved.
  • 13 to 19 November 2026
    Six barrier-discharge periods in CFX: 576 823 s of CPU time, 6.4 days on one core.
  • 12 to 20 November 2026
    Six periods in OpenFOAM, run in a Linux container; comparison with CFX periods 1 to 4 within 7.2 % in peak current.
  • 20 November 2026
    Technical report on the thesis model issued (54 pages). The jet run on the original mesh breaks down at 4.38 µs, where the ionisation front is thinner than the cells; the mesh is refined to 20 µm along the jet's path.
  • Now (23 November 2026)
    One CFX run continues on the refined jet mesh, on four processor cores: after about 31,000 time steps it has reached 4.88 µs of the 7.30 µs voltage rise, past the 4.38 µs where the coarse mesh broke down. Electrons multiply inside the capillary; the plasma has not yet left it. The OpenFOAM model, on the same mesh, shows the same ionised region: at 3.80 µs the peak electron densities are 1.43 × 1013 per m3 in CFX and 1.27 × 1013 per m3 in OpenFOAM. No jet first-pulse result exists yet, and the jet is not reproduced.
  • Next
    The CFX run continues up the voltage rise; then the jet pulse is compared with the thesis's figures. No completion date is set.

Documentation: technical reports (54 pages on the thesis model) and a 34-page explanatory guide to low-temperature plasma for engineers new to the subject. Electron data: BOLSIG+ (Hagelaar and Pitchford) with its bundled LXCat-based cross-section database.
